intro: Prokofiev fits a whole symphony into less than a quarter of an hour: a brisk Allegro, a singing Larghetto, a Gavotte and a racing finale. Nicolai Malko conducts the Philharmonia Orchestra.

sections.label: A · Allegro: Haydn with sharp elbows

cues.title: Violins and dry bassoons
cues.text: The Allegro packs its argument into a short sonata-form movement. A dashing first tune shares the stage with a second in which staccato bassoons accompany the first violins. Prokofiev keeps the instruments of a Haydn orchestra and lets their harmony misbehave.
cues.evidence: Andrew Mellor, Philharmonia programme, 10 April 2025, p. 4, describes the first movement and its bassoon accompaniment. Gerard McBurney’s Boosey & Hawkes note gives the classical-sized instrumentation. https://philharmonia-assets.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/uploads/2025/04/03122720/10.04.25_RFH_online.pdf; https://www.boosey.com/cr/music/Serge-Prokofieff-Classical-Symphony-in-D-Symphony-No-1/4801
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano stays behind
cues.text: In the summer of 1917 Prokofiev leaves his piano behind and works in the country near Petrograd. He composes much of the symphony on long walks, testing whether orchestral ideas can come more freely when his fingers have no keyboard to dictate them.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev’s autobiography, quoted by Herbert Glass in the Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: summer 1917, the country near Petrograd, composing without a piano and during long walks. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical

cues.title: A singing Larghetto
cues.text: The Larghetto stretches out a melody where the Allegro kept changing the subject. Its leisurely pace occupies almost as much of this performance as the first movement.
cues.evidence: The four-movement order is printed on RCA Victor LM-2092; Herbert Glass describes the songful Larghetto. The two movements occupy approximately four minutes each in this transfer. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical; https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-7-classical-symphony_sergei-prokofiev-nicolai-malko-philharmoni
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Haydn in Petrograd
cues.text: Prokofiev imagines Haydn alive in his own century, keeping his style while admitting something new. The symphony is completed in September 1917; Prokofiev conducts its première in Petrograd on 21 April 1918, with the October Revolution between those two dates.
cues.evidence: Andrew Mellor, Philharmonia programme, 10 April 2025, p. 4: completion on 10 September 1917, première on 21 April 1918, and Prokofiev’s autobiographical account of Haydn. Herbert Glass identifies the composer as conductor. https://philharmonia-assets.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/uploads/2025/04/03122720/10.04.25_RFH_online.pdf; https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical

cues.title: The Gavotte’s crooked bow
cues.text: A gavotte takes the place normally occupied by a minuet. Its courtly steps survive a succession of unexpected chords. Prokofiev also plays this little dance on the piano as a recital encore.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass describes the Gavotte’s harmonic surprises; Andrew Mellor identifies the eighteenth-century dance and Prokofiev’s use of it as a piano encore. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical; https://philharmonia-assets.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/uploads/2025/04/03122720/10.04.25_RFH_online.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Molto vivace
cues.text: The finale sends its tunes racing through the orchestra. Prokofiev throws away an earlier ending and writes this one afresh, setting himself the task of avoiding minor chords.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev’s autobiography, quoted by Herbert Glass, describes replacing the original finale and trying to avoid minor chords. The movement marking is Molto vivace. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First and last
cues.text: The original LP places this first symphony beside Prokofiev’s Seventh, his last. The Philharmonia Orchestra and Nicolai Malko play both: fourteen minutes from the young composer beside the final symphony completed in 1952.
cues.evidence: RCA Victor LM-2092 sleeve and Irvine Kolodin’s notes identify both symphonies, performers and the Seventh’s completion in 1952. https://archive.org/download/lp_symphony-no-7-classical-symphony_sergei-prokofiev-nicolai-malko-philharmoni/lp_symphony-no-7-classical-symphony_sergei-prokofiev-nicolai-malko-philharmoni_djvu.txt

composer.born: 27 April (15 April Old Style) 1891; Prokofiev himself gave 23 April, Sontsovka, Ukraine, then Russian Empire
composer.epithet: He gave Romeo and Juliet its singing strings and the piano some of the twentieth century’s sharpest teeth.
facts: Glière at Sontsovka, 1902–03; St Petersburg Conservatory, 1904–14
Russia · United States · Bavaria · Paris; settled in Moscow in 1936
The Love for Three Oranges · Romeo and Juliet · Cinderella · War and Peace
Seven symphonies, five piano concertos and nine completed piano sonatas

quote.text: It seemed to me that if Haydn had lived into our own time, he would have kept his way of writing while taking in something new.
quote.source: Prokofiev, short Autobiography (1941), recalling the summer of 1917; our translation

composer.background:
At Sontsovka, the Ukrainian estate his father managed, Prokofiev grew up hearing his mother play Beethoven and Chopin. She wrote down his first piano pieces. A trip to the Moscow opera in 1900 gave the eight-year-old an ambition of his own: The Giant, an opera for the family to perform at home. Sergei Taneyev recommended proper lessons, and Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka, teaching the boy who was already filling manuscript books.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen with a bundle of scores. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Lyadov harmony and counterpoint; later Anna Esipova took charge of his piano playing. Nikolai Tcherepnin taught conducting and encouraged his taste for Haydn and Mozart. His fellow student Nikolai Myaskovsky became the friend to whom he sent scores and complaints for the rest of his life. In the final piano competition of 1914, Prokofiev played his own First Concerto. He won the Rubinstein Prize: a grand piano.
